\chapter{Nice to Meet You}
\label{ch:la-nice-to-meet-you}

\section[volup est convēnisse]{volup est convēnisse — the phrase Latin uses instead of a fixed idiom}

\label{lesson:LA-C21-volup-est-convenisse}



\begin{quote}
Every modern language in this course has one fixed phrase for \textquotedblleft{}nice to meet you.\textquotedblright{} Latin, honestly, does \textbf{not} — but it has something better: a real line from a Roman comedy that does the job.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Plautus}'s comedy \emph{Miles Gloriosus} (Act 2, Scene 3) gives us a real line that does exactly this work: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Tē, {[}name{]}, volup est convēnisse\textquotedblright{}} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you, {[}name{]}, {[}it{]} is-a-pleasure to-have-met},\textquotedblright{} or naturally, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it's a pleasure to have met you, {[}name{]}.}\textquotedblright{} Break it down:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{volup} — an old, indeclinable word for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{pleasant, pleasing}\textquotedblright{} (functioning here the way \emph{iuvat}, \textquotedblleft{}it pleases,\textquotedblright{} would)
  \item \textbf{est} — \textquotedblleft{}{[}it{]} \textbf{is}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{convēnisse} — the \textbf{perfect infinitive} of \emph{convenīre}, \textquotedblleft{}to come together, to meet\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to have met}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Put together: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to have met {[}you{]} is a pleasure.}\textquotedblright{} This is a genuine, attested line — not a modern reconstruction.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}volup est convēnisse\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}it's a pleasure to have met you\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pieces — volup (pleasant) + est (is) + convēnisse (to have met)
  \item the grammar — convēnisse is a perfect infinitive
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Classical Latin have one single fixed idiom for \textquotedblleft{}nice to meet you\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — Romans expressed the sentiment according to context.) What real, attested phrase can do the job, and where does it come from? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Volup est convēnisse\textquotedblright{}}, literally \textquotedblleft{}to have met {[}you{]} is a pleasure\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{Plautus}, \emph{Miles Gloriosus}.) What kind of infinitive is \textbf{convēnisse}? (\textbf{Perfect} — \textquotedblleft{}to have met.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tē volup est convēnisse]{Useful phrase, honest context}

\label{lesson:LA-C21-meeting-phrase-context}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Volup est convēnisse} is genuinely Roman. Now place it in its scene so you know exactly what that evidence does—and does not—prove.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
In \emph{Miles Gloriosus}, Sceledrus and Palaestrio are fellow slaves who already know one another. The line welcomes a \textbf{chance encounter}. It does not document a fixed formula that Romans always used when introduced to a stranger for the first time.

The phrase still expresses the right sentiment: \textquotedblleft{}to have met you is a pleasure.\textquotedblright{} Use it as an attested way to do that conversational work, while remembering that Classical Latin has no single fixed counterpart to Spanish \emph{encantado} or German \emph{freut mich}.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Modern spoken-Latin guides may teach \textbf{mihi pergrātum est tē convenīre}: \textquotedblleft{}it is very pleasing to me to meet you.\textquotedblright{} Its grammar is sound, but the formula does not occur in surviving classical texts. It is useful modern Latin, not direct evidence of Roman conversational convention.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}volup est convēnisse\textquotedblright{} — classically attested
  \item its scene — a chance encounter between people already acquainted
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mihi pergrātum est tē convenīre\textquotedblright{} — grammatical, but modern
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the Plautine line a first-time introduction? (\textbf{No — it is a chance encounter between acquaintances.}) Is it still genuinely attested? (\textbf{Yes.}) Is \textbf{mihi pergrātum est tē convenīre} bad grammar? (\textbf{No.}) Is it classically attested? (\textbf{No — it is a modern spoken-Latin formula.})
\end{tcolorbox}
